notes.title: ASINH is LN(|x|+SQRT(x*x+1)) with every step stored, so small inputs lose their digits
notes.statement: ASINH is not the correctly rounded inverse hyperbolic sine. Its answers are those of SIGN(x)*LN(|x|+SQRT(x*x+1)), with x*x, the +1, the SQRT and the |x|+root each rounded to 64 bits and then to 53 bits before the next step, and the LN rounded to binary64. That route loses most of the digits of a small input: once x*x+1 rounds to 1, the answer is LN of |x|+1 after rounding, so it moves in steps of about 2.2E-16. ASINH(-1.4901631254755754E-16) is -2.22E-16, about 1.5 times the true value, and in the recorded rows every |x| up to 1.05E-16, including every subnormal, gives 0 on either sign. At the other end the x*x overflows: answers are finite up to the largest recorded input below it, 9.23E153, and #NUM! from the next recorded input, 2.38E154, although the true value there is about 356. In Excel build 20430 this route reproduces all 4,534 recorded rows (3,017 distinct inputs): 3,427 numbers and 1,107 #NUM!. The correctly rounded asinh matches only 1,224 of the 3,427.
notes.basis: All 4,534 rows of two recorded sets, 3,017 and 1,517 rows, from Excel build 20430. The route was recomputed independently in exact rational arithmetic with a correctly rounded LN, and matched every row. The stored steps matter on 5 of the rows (3 distinct inputs): the same formula in plain binary64 misses exactly those 5.
notes.inferred: That Excel's code is this expression, in this order, is inferred; what is measured is that the route reproduces every recorded row. The overflow boundary at |x| = 2^512, about 1.34E154, is inferred from x*x overflowing there: the recorded rows only bracket it, between 9.23E153 and 2.38E154. Excel reads a subnormal written to a cell back as 0, so the 0 at subnormal inputs may come from that step and not from this route.

notes.title: On basis 1 COUPDAYS walks back from maturity by its own rule, not COUPPCD to COUPNCD
notes.statement: On basis 1 (actual/actual) COUPDAYS does not always equal COUPNCD minus COUPPCD. Its rule: start at maturity and step back by 12/frequency months. Each step keeps the day of the month and clamps it to the length of the target month, and the clamped date is the start of the next step, so passing through February lowers the day for every earlier date. Stop at the last date still after settlement, call it next. The answer is the number of actual days from one period before next up to next, and this last step keeps month ends: if next is the last day of its month, the start is the last day of its month. On the other bases the answer is 360/frequency (bases 0, 2, 4) or 365/frequency (basis 3). With this rule, all 5,584 recorded rows match (4,072 distinct inputs): 5,568 numbers and 16 #NUM!, from Excel builds 20131 and 20430. Of the 967 basis 1 rows, 81 (49 distinct inputs) differ from the day count between the dates of a schedule anchored on maturity with month ends kept. For maturity 1998-06-30 with semi-annual coupons, COUPDAYS(35748,35976,2,1) is 183, from 1997-06-30 to 1997-12-30; the anchored schedule gives 184. In one recorded case all three functions were read on the same inputs: COUPNCD(44043,2958465,2,1) less COUPPCD is 44196 - 44012 = 184, and COUPDAYS is 183.
notes.basis: All 5,584 rows of three recorded sets: 3,012 and 1,512 rows from build 20430, 1,060 from build 20131. The rule was recomputed independently from the calendar and matched all 5,566 number rows with settlement at serial 61 or later, on every basis. The other two number rows have settlement 0 and basis 0, and read 180. In a study of 42 ways to walk and measure the schedule, this was the only one to match all 965 rows with basis exactly 1.
notes.inferred: The rule reproduces every recorded row; that Excel's code works this way is inferred. For basis 1 no settlement or maturity before serial 61, where Excel's calendar differs from the Gregorian one, is in the recorded rows.

notes.title: On basis 0 COUPDAYSNC is not always COUPDAYS minus COUPDAYBS
notes.statement: On basis 0 (US 30/360), COUPDAYSNC is P - A. A is COUPDAYBS, the accrued days. P is a 30/360 count between the actual previous and next coupon dates, with day 31 and the last day of February both counted as day 30. COUPDAYS on basis 0 is always 360/frequency, but P need not be: when a coupon falls on the last day of February and maturity is not a month end, P can be 88, 89 or 92 for a quarter and 178 or 182 for a half year. So COUPDAYSNC(39923,50919,4,0), with coupons 2009-02-28 and 2009-05-29, is 39: P is 89 and A is 50, where 90 - 50 would give 40. With no coupon date before settlement in Excel's calendar, the period starts at serial 0: COUPDAYSNC(33,400,2,0) is 1, and for settlement 61, maturity 456 and annual coupons COUPDAYBS plus COUPDAYSNC is 90, not 360. This rule matches all 1,664 recorded number rows on basis 0, 733 of them chosen near February, month ends and the start of the calendar.
notes.basis: 1,664 recorded rows with a number answer on basis 0, from builds 20131, 20430 and 20527, recomputed independently from the calendar. An implementation of these rules matches all 33,504 selected readings of the six coupon functions. Fictitious 1900-02-29 is not a month end here.
notes.inferred: The split into P and A reproduces every row; that Excel's code forms these two counts is inferred. For the February cases in this note only COUPDAYSNC is recorded: their A comes from the rule, not from a COUPDAYBS reading.

notes.title: Below 0.5, ERF is a stored (4, 5) rational from a table not yet identified
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, ERF.PRECISE for |x| < 0.5 is x*N(t)/D(t) with t = RN(x*x), p = RN(x*N), y = RN(p/D), and N and D Horner sums in t in which every product and every sum is RN. N has degree 4 and D degree 5, and the coefficients read off Excel's answers, order 0 upward, are N: 0x3ff1df5e70c7956b, 0x3fc201d8627a7d2c, 0x3fa6f289d165b303, 0x3f5d93a5813e372c, 0x3f2932767df264b2; D: 0x3fefada15778ece6, 0x3fdd191aca8d2499, 0x3fb79f85ba68803e, 0x3f856de5da86af12, 0x3f4609751b5b6488, 0x3ef4f20a473a5ab0. The rational stops at 0.5 itself. It equals erf to a flat 9E-17 up to 0.5, and its error climbs at once beyond, so 0.5 is its design interval and not Cody's 0.46875. No published table has been matched: Cody's 1969 rational is refuted by its linear terms, and Cephes has the same shape with different ratios. Evidence record EV-DIST-0026, which predates this note, attributes ERF.PRECISE and ERFC.PRECISE to the a < 1 branches of the NSWC GRATIO routine and says no coefficient table exists; below 0.5 this note replaces that attribution. Because every step rounds, answers need not be correctly rounded: of the 654 recorded rows of build 20131 in [0.25, 0.5), 400 differ from the correctly rounded erf, by up to 3 units, and small arguments can be 1 unit high, as below. ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE below 0.5 are 1 less this value, and GAUSS at tiny arguments takes half of it at its stored z/sqrt(2).
notes.basis: All 618,225 recorded ERF.PRECISE rows with |x| < 0.5 match; they were only scored, never used to read the coefficients, and ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE match every recorded row in that range. Two fresh sets of 60,000 random doubles below 0.5 (Excel build 20527) match 59,996 and 59,982; the second was asked after the constants were fixed, and 17 of its 18 misses are in [0.25, 0.5). With every step stored, 223 of 38,000 rows at 19 sites stay unexplained; the other store placements leave 568 to 1,244. 2,000 consecutive doubles below 0.5 match 1,988, and 2,000 from 0.5 up match 858, chance level, which places the cut.
notes.inferred: That the legacy ERF(x) shares this body is inferred: ERF.PRECISE, ERFC and ERFC.PRECISE rows were scored in full, and for ERF itself the record holds only nine non-zero single-argument inputs below 0.5 (build 19929), all equal to the rational.

notes.title: Above 0.5, ERFC rounds x*x before the exponential, so the tail drifts by hundreds of units
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, ERFC for x >= 0.5 behaves as Q = E*F with z = RN(x*x) and E = exp(-z) stored to binary64, then multiplied by a factor F that is not identified. So the rounding error of x*x reaches the answer at full size. At x = 26.543000000000003, x*x exceeds z by 4.64E-14, which at the size of this answer is about 212 units, and Excel's answer is 212 units above the correctly rounded erfc. Near x = 5.93 the same effect is 23 units. For small x, where x*x is exact or nearly so, the answer stays within a few units.
notes.basis: 220,000 Excel answers from 0.5 to 26.5 (build 20527) compared with E times the true exp(x*x)*erfc(x). With z = RN(x*x) and E stored, the residual stays within about 10 units of 2^-53 at every x. At x = 24 the exact exp(-x*x) spreads with a standard deviation of 287 units, Cody's and fdlibm's fractional splits of x*x spread the same, and plain binary64 x*x leaves outliers of up to 1,024 units.
notes.inferred: F is not a closed form: y = RN(E*RN(F)) with any offset matches 40% of answers at best. Its noise tracks about a dozen smooth curves, consistent with two polynomials of degree about 8 in x with shapes near Cephes' erfc P and Q, but that is a reading of shape only, and no table has been matched.

notes.title: FLOOR rounds its quotient to 15 digits first, so the result can pass the number
notes.statement: FLOOR behaves as s times the floor of number/s, where the quotient is first rounded to 15 significant decimal digits and the final product is taken in binary64. A quotient just under an integer therefore counts as that integer, and the result can exceed the number: FLOOR(0.9999999999999999,0.1) is 1. Once the quotient has more than 15 significant digits the step moves it by more than one unit, so an exact multiple can change: FLOOR(4503599627370496,2) is 4503599627370500.
notes.basis: All 931 recorded rows with normal nonzero arguments and a number answer, Excel build 20430, recomputed for this note from the recorded inputs; the 1,335 rows of that capture also hold errors, zero and subnormal cases. On the 945 rows that include subnormal quotients, the plain route matches 857 and an exact floor 848. A separate 120 literal calls in build 20527 agree. The rule was first stated from readings of this family, so these counts are in sample.
notes.inferred: That Excel's code rounds to 15 digits this way is inferred from the fit. Whether FLOOR.MATH and FLOOR.PRECISE take the same step has not been read.

notes.title: From 10 up, GAMMA is a Stirling product of stored stages, and its error grows with x
notes.statement: From x = 10, GAMMA behaves as sqrt(2 pi) x^x exp(-x) / sqrt(x) w with stored stages: x^2, x^4, x^8 and so on by binary powering of floor(x/2), stored ln x, exponent and exponential for the fraction of x/2, stored exp(-x), an unstored square root, and each outer product stored. The cumulative answer is RN(r*S) with S the stored forward sum, and the density RN(r*a)/x, the division last; with a scale, y = RN(x/beta) comes first. So GAMMALN's own error is in every answer: at shape 2 the constant is GAMMALN(3), one unit above stored ln 2 (FN-GAMMALN-001).

notes.title: A direct error stops these array functions; the same error in an array or cell is an element
notes.statement: An error written directly as an argument of these functions is the answer for the whole call. It is not placed in the result: HSTACK(1,#VALUE!) is #VALUE!, not a row holding 1 and an error, and TAKE(#N/A,0) is #N/A. With MAP the LAMBDA does not run at all: MAP(NA(),LAMBDA(xx,IFERROR(xx,3))) is #N/A. The same error inside an array, or in a referenced cell, is an ordinary element: MAP({#N/A},LAMBDA(xx,3)) is 3, and HSTACK(Data!C1,{1;2}) with #N/A in Data!C1 is a 2 by 2 array with #N/A in its first column. TOCOL and TOROW show the difference with ignore 2: TOCOL(#N/A,2) is #N/A, while TOCOL({#N/A},2) drops the error, has nothing left, and is #CALC!. EXPAND is an exception on the cell side: EXPAND(Data!C1,2,2,"pad") is #N/A for the whole call. BYROW and BYCOL check the direct error first too: BYROW(#N/A,#VALUE!) is #N/A, while BYROW({#N/A},2), where 2 is not a LAMBDA, is #VALUE!.

notes.title: IFS and SWITCH pass on the selected value whole, and later arrays do not lift the call
notes.statement: Once a scalar test selects a result, array arguments after it have no effect on the shape: IFS(TRUE,1,{FALSE,TRUE},{2,3}) and SWITCH(2,2,1,{1,2},3) each return one 1, not an array, and SWITCH("A","a",1,{"A","A"},2) returns 1 because the match ignores case. The selected value itself is passed on as it is. A selected reference stays a reference: ISBLANK(IFS(TRUE,Data!Z1)) is TRUE over an empty cell. A selected LAMBDA shows as #CALC! in the cell, IFS(TRUE,LAMBDA(xx,xx)), and a selected array of LAMBDAs as #CALC! in each cell. A test that is not TRUE or FALSE gives #VALUE! in the shape of its result: IFS("2",{"hit","hit"}) is {#VALUE!,#VALUE!}. A direct error as the SWITCH expression stays one error: SWITCH(#VALUE!,1,{1,2},0) is #VALUE!.

notes.title: MOD with tiny operands gives wrong signs and #NUM!, by a rule that fits every recorded row
notes.statement: MOD(n,d) takes the exact remainder r of n by d and adds d when their signs differ. Three things change when r is subnormal and its sign differs from d's. The result is #NUM! when |n/d| is 2^26 or more, or when d's low part under a Veltkamp split at 2^27 + 1 is subnormal. Otherwise, when |r| is below 2^-1026, the result is |d| + |r| with d's sign: the remainder is added where it should be taken away. A larger r takes the ordinary step. Any subnormal final result is #NUM!. So MOD(-(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, 2^-983) returns +(1+121*2^-52)*2^-983, and MOD(2^-983, -(1+120*2^-52)*2^-983) returns #NUM!, where the exact answers are ordinary numbers.

notes.title: ROUND counts digits in 32 bits, and the count wraps
notes.statement: ROUND cuts num_digits toward zero to a 32-bit integer D, limited to +/-2147483647, and keeps k = D + e + 1 significant digits, where e is the decimal exponent of |number| and the sum is computed in 32 bits. k of 15 or more keeps the 15-digit reading of the number; k below 0 gives 0. A large positive num_digits therefore wraps to no digits at all: for a number near 1.1E14, 2147483617 returns the number and 2147483635 returns 0. notes.title: The variance family uses raw moments with stored steps, and two tests switch it to a centered sum
notes.statement: With RN(v) meaning v rounded to 64 bits on the x87 unit and then stored to binary64, S the running RN sum of the n values and Q the running RN sum of RN(x*x), the sample variance is RN(RN(Q - RN(RN(S*S)/n))/(n-1)) and the population variance RN(RN(RN(n*Q) - RN(S*S))/RN(n*n)). Excel then uses a centered sum instead, adding RN(d*d) with d = RN(x - mean) and dividing by n-1 or n, when either of two stored tests holds: RN(RN(RN(S*S)/n)/Q) > 0.99, or RN(variance*1000) <= |RN(S/n)|. The STDEV functions are the root of this, rounded to 64 bits and then stored. So the answer depends on which path a call takes: the first two VAR.S calls below differ by a few input steps in two arguments, the first passes the 0.99 test and is correctly rounded, and the second takes the raw moments and lands 76 units high. The next pair shows the size test: scaling the inputs by 4 leaves the first path.
notes.basis: All 14,679 recorded rows of the twelve functions match: VAR.S, VAR.P, VAR, VARP, VARA, VARPA, STDEV.S, STDEV.P, STDEV, STDEVP, STDEVA and STDEVPA. Six of those rows separate the stored steps from plain binary64. 910 fresh scalar variance readings (Excel build 20527) replay exactly in rational arithmetic. Four cancellation edges were bisected to adjacent inputs; sixteen triples chosen to separate the stored ratio from 0.99*Q and from a division by 0.99 all agree with the ratio, where 0.99*Q misses all 16 and the division 14. Seven of eight magnitude brackets reach adjacent inputs, and sixteen chosen roots all need the 64-bit root followed by a store.
notes.inferred: These tests were located with scalar arguments in separate cells; that the same edges hold for ranges and arrays is inferred, and their readings have not been taken. RN(variance*1000) <= |mean| is not separated from the rearrangement variance <= |mean|/1000. That a raw moment which overflows also takes the centered sum is inferred from recorded answers that stay finite.

notes.title: On basis 1 the fictitious 1900-02-29 is not a leap day, and YEARFRAC takes serial 0 as a date
notes.statement: Excel's calendar holds a 29 February 1900, serial 60, that never existed. On basis 1 (actual/actual) it does not make 1900 a leap year: YEARFRAC(59,60,1) is 1/365, where the real 1904-02-29 gives YEARFRAC(1520,1521,1) = 1/366. Serial 0 is accepted as a date: YEARFRAC(0,5,0) is 5/360 and YEARFRAC(0,60,1) is 60/365. Reversed dates give the same answer as in order. ACCRINTM, DISC, INTRATE, PRICEDISC and RECEIVED take the same 365 and 366 on those dates: DISC(59,60,99,100,1) is about 3.65 and DISC(1520,1521,99,100,1) about 3.66.
notes.basis: 19 YEARFRAC readings around serial 60 and the 1904, 2000 and 2004 leap days, 35 readings with serial 0 on all five bases, and 3 readings each from five financial functions.
